title: Greedy Best-First: Beat Lima’s Streets Fast!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First race from start to goal across real street-like graph nodes in Barranco, Lima. The algorithm prioritizes the most promising next step using a heuristic, often finding quick routes and showing where it can get misled.
ig_caption:
🚦 **Greedy Best-First in Lima (Barranco)!** 🗺️⚡

In this visualization, each intersection is a **graph node** and each road segment is an **edge**. Greedy Best-First uses a **priority queue** to expand the node with the smallest **heuristic estimate h(n)** (distance-to-go), so it “chases” the goal rather than building an optimal path from the start.

📌 **Graph theory angle:** We’re effectively running a **best-first graph search** over a street-map-inspired graph, where the heuristic (e.g., straight-line distance from GPS coords) guides exploration. Because it doesn’t combine path cost g(n) with h(n), it can be blazing fast—but it may commit to locally attractive routes that later become suboptimal. 🎯

✅ Want the shortest-path behavior instead? Try swapping to A* in your next experiment and compare expansions.

👉 **Comment “LIMA”** and tell me: should the heuristic be **optimistic** or **conservative** for better results on real streets? 🔍
fb_caption:
🚙💡 **Greedy Best-First Pathfinding in Lima (Barranco)!**

This reel visualizes how a graph search moves through a street-map-like network: intersections become nodes, streets become edges, and the algorithm selects the next node using only a heuristic estimate of distance to the goal. Greedy Best-First is a classic **best-first search strategy**—fast when the heuristic matches reality, but potentially shortsighted when the map geometry misleads it.

📣 If you learn something from this, share it with a friend who loves algorithms and drop a question in the comments for a follow-up comparison to A*!

Greedy Best-First algorithm visualization on real street-map style graphs! 🌎⚡ In this YouTube Shorts, we run **Greedy Best-First search** over Lima (Barranco) intersections, using a heuristic (straight-line distance) to guide expansions. You’ll see how priority-queue selection works, how graph nodes/edges model real roads, and why Greedy Best-First can be quick but not always optimal.
